The remote-meeting question decides whether residents can attend or comment on board meetings from home, and no position has been settled.

Common victualler and 2023 miscellaneous license renewals passed unanimously, and the board agreed to discuss making a certificate of good standing an explicit licensing policy.
The board reviewed the remote work policy and the appointment policy line by line; the remote work policy returns next week after minor changes.
The board appointed three members to the new 300th Anniversary Committee and waived first refusal on a Chapter 61 parcel, both unanimously.
The town manager reported on the Lufa Farms project, whose tax increment financing agreement would need a vote at annual town meeting.

why_it_matters: A tax increment financing agreement for Lufa Farms would change how new tax revenue from the project is treated, and residents would be asked to vote on it at annual town meeting.
The remote work and appointment policies set how town staff and volunteer board members are chosen and employed, and the appointment policy is likely to be approved next week.
watch_next: The Select Board meeting on Dec 20, 2022, where the remote work policy returns, the appointment policy is likely to be approved, and the ARPA discussion is scheduled.
The annual town meeting vote on any Lufa Farms tax increment financing agreement.

what_happened.line: The Select Board adopted a single tax rate for FY2023 on the principal assessor's recommendation, passing 5-0.
The board approved a homeowner's access to town land at Palmetto Road for a septic replacement, unanimously, under a right-of-entry agreement.
The board voted not to pass over Article 8, the firefighter on-call buyback, so it goes to Special Town Meeting with a motion still to be drafted.
The board ratified the town manager's appointment of a conservation administrator, 4-1.
The chair was directed to build an ARPA process from the evaluation criteria, separating traditional capital requests from other uses, and return in December.

why_it_matters: Keeping a single rate means residential and commercial property are taxed at the same rate, so the split-rate shift of tax burden onto commercial property did not happen for FY2023 bills.

The firefighter buyback article will reach Special Town Meeting without a cost estimate, because the town manager said the payroll history needed to produce one could not be assembled in time, so voters may be asked to decide without a price.
The ARPA process the board sets in December will decide whether remaining federal relief money is used for capital projects the town would otherwise fund itself.
watch_next: December 6 meeting: the right-of-entry agreement for the Palmetto Road septic work is to be signed, and the chair is to bring back the ARPA process.
Special Town Meeting: Article 8 on the firefighter buyback, with the motion still to be drafted.

what_happened.line: The Select Board went through the special town meeting warrant article by article, recommending approval of some, disapproval of others, and deferring several.
The board deferred Article 1, the budget adjustment, until the final new growth number is known.
A recommendation of disapproval on Article 12, the Ritter windows, failed on a tie, and the board then moved to defer it to town meeting.
The board recommended disapproval of moving town meeting to April, 4-0, and of the capital line item veto article, 3-1.
The Il Forno hearing on adding a permanent structure was continued to November 1, with the applicant to submit floor plans.

why_it_matters: Several warrant articles reach special town meeting without a Select Board recommendation, so residents voting there will have less guidance on spending items.
The Article 1 budget adjustment and the Article 4 funding both depend on a new growth figure not yet certified, and that figure sets how much money is available without new taxes.
The firefighter on-call time buyback was deferred partly because its cost to the retirement system is unknown, so its effect on the town budget, mostly taxes, is not yet stated.
watch_next: The Il Forno alteration-of-premises hearing resumes November 1 at 7:15 pm, when floor plans are due.
The new growth certification, which the board said it is waiting on before recommending Articles 1 and 4.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted 4-0 to support the water district's plan for a pilot study of the Hickory Hills well.
Most of the meeting was the water district's presentation on reactivating the well; lake residents raised concerns about the lake, the shallow well and the easement.
The district said the pilot would be paid from its system enhancement fund of connection fees, with later treatment through state loans and rates, not a betterment.
The board voted unanimously to authorize the town manager to file an asset management grant application with MassDEP.
The board ratified a heavy equipment operator appointment; the 300th anniversary charge and a letter to Brixmore on donation bins return for a vote next week.

why_it_matters: The Hickory Hills well pilot is the first step toward a possible treatment plant, and the minutes say later treatment would be paid through state loans and water rates rather than a betterment, so it may reach water bills.
The pilot is funded from connection fees rather than the town budget, but a full treatment plant was described as a larger cost the district is not pursuing now.
watch_next: The Select Board's vote on the revised 300th anniversary committee charge, expected next week.
The town manager's draft letter to Brixmore about litter and the donation bins, due for the board next week.

In a joint workshop with the Capital Planning Committee, the board listed candidate uses for ARPA funds but made no spending decision.
The board agreed to send an ARPA proposal request to all departments and boards, with a September 30 deadline, but took no vote.
The finance director reported FY22 collections above estimates, and an estimated free cash above last year's certification.
The board will send the chair and town manager to the next School Committee meeting to voice concerns about the walking and busing policy.

why_it_matters: ARPA money is one-time federal funding, and the proposals departments file by the September 30 deadline will shape which projects compete for it and what is left for the tax-funded capital plan.

Free cash above the state's guidance range gives Town Meeting more room to use it, and changes to school walking and busing policy would affect families' daily routines and school transportation costs.
watch_next: The September 30 deadline for department and board ARPA proposals, after which the board is expected to prioritize the project list.

Election officers and police at polling places affect how the elections budget is spent, which registrars described as stretched thin.

The board said the Finance Committee may use town counsel on a bylaw to amend the capital plan, if it brings a draft; members said they oppose the bylaw on the merits.

what_happened.line: The Select Board reached consensus of four on term limits: four consecutive terms, then a full-term break, with the policy to go to other boards for input first.
The board agreed to interview incumbents and new applicants together and not to advertise incumbent reappointment bids.
The board approved its FY2023 goals as modified and the town manager's FY2023 goals.
The board approved a conditional one-day alcohol license for Conrad's, tied to proof of insurance and a revised site plan.
The town manager listed possible fall town meeting articles, including assessor inspection funding, a prior-year payroll invoice and a compensation study consultant.

why_it_matters: Term limits and the reappointment process decide how long residents can serve on town boards and how openings are posted, so the draft policy may change who can seek a seat.
The possible fall town meeting articles are spending requests that residents may be asked to vote on.
watch_next: The draft term limit policy, to be circulated to town boards for input before the Select Board finalizes it.
The warrant for the fall special town meeting, which may carry the articles the town manager named.

what_happened.line: The Select Board approved a commemorative policy with 25 years set as the age factor, and it will be a separate policy for naming things after people.
The board postponed transfers of foreclosed properties to the start of the next fiscal year in July and asked for acreage and valuation information.
A draft tailings policy for uncashed checks was held for a second reading, with a vote expected at the next meeting.
The one-day liquor license insurance requirement was sent back for sample language and limits, and a five-year history of licenses was requested.
The board ratified the annual town election warrant and its own signing of it, and a member will draft a rule allowing election signs on town property on election day only.

why_it_matters: The tailings policy would set a cutoff for cashing town checks, so residents or vendors holding old uncashed checks could see them cancelled and the funds closed out at year end.
The foreclosed-property transfers, the insurance requirement for one-day liquor licenses and the election-sign rule all affect how town land and events are managed, and each is still undecided.
watch_next: The tailings policy returns at the next Select Board meeting for a vote after its second reading.
The foreclosed-property transfers return at the start of the next fiscal year in July.

what_happened.line: The Select Board ratified the town manager's appointments of a police sergeant and a DPW director, both without opposition.
The board held a public hearing on the plan creating a facilities director position; no second hearing was set, and the finance committee will hear it Thursday.
The board approved the public employee committee agreement effective July 1, 2022, with no one opposed.
A motion to move three foreclosed parcels to the conservation commission was withdrawn, and the item returns next meeting with acreages, land values and abutter interest.
The board added Article 17, cemetery lot proceeds, to the town meeting consent calendar and appointed a resident member to the Architectural Preservation District Commission.

why_it_matters: The facilities director plan and the public employee agreement change how town staff are organised and what the town's labor agreements commit it to, and both reach the town budget, mostly taxes.

The consent calendar lets town meeting vote on routine articles, including transfers to stabilization funds and the sewer, water and solid waste appropriations, in one motion, so a resident who wants one discussed has to ask for it to be pulled.
The foreclosed parcels would leave general town control if transferred, and the board has not yet been given their size or value.
watch_next: The finance committee hears the facilities director plan on Thursday.
The conservation land transfer returns at the board's next meeting with acreages, land values and abutter interest.

what_happened.line: The Select Board held a site visit on Flat Hill Road and Cortland Circle to see flooding and drainage problems firsthand; no vote was taken.
Residents described flooding that they said goes back to the 1990s development, including basement water, constantly running sump pumps and failed earlier fixes.
The town's consulting engineer said high groundwater limits stormwater fixes on the road shoulders, and that the cost would far outweigh the benefit.
The engineer will get electronic copies of the original development drainage plans and review them with precipitation data before recommending a fix.
No further survey is needed now; investigating the plans and groundwater comes next.

why_it_matters: Neighbors on Flat Hill Road and Cortland Circle have no fix yet, and any drainage work the town later proposes would be a public works cost that could come before voters as a budget item.

Residents elsewhere along the Beaver Brook and Page Street drainage path raised concern that moving water downstream could worsen conditions for them, so a fix may affect more than the streets visited.
watch_next: The engineer's review of the original drainage plans and precipitation data, and the recommendation that follows.

Whether the town provides trash service on private roads is unsettled and tied to the hauler's contract, so residents on those roads have no answer yet.

In a joint vote with the housing authority, the board unanimously appointed Wayne Caron to the tenant seat on the Lunenburg Housing Authority.
The board agreed on an order of FY2023 priorities to put to legislators, led by the Flat Hill Road culvert and old primary school abatement, and dropped two candidates.
The board opened the annual town meeting warrant for January 12, 2022 and set it to close March 21, 2022 at 4 p.m.
The board approved changes to the emergency paid sick leave policy and adopted a revised charge for the Municipal Building Design Committee.

why_it_matters: The boulder dispute may lead to a court case, and the minutes leave the cost of filing and any court costs unclear, so it could draw on town funds.

The priority list sets which capital projects, such as the culvert and the old primary school abatement, the town asks state legislators to fund, and that affects what residents may later be asked to pay for locally.
The open warrant is how articles reach the March town meeting, where residents vote on spending.
watch_next: The town meeting warrant opens January 12, 2022 and closes March 21, 2022 at 4 p.m.
Policy meetings on liquor regulations, boot drives and a commemorative policy are to be scheduled.
